parole.testo: First attested as а́ккула f (ákkula) in 1747 and 1789, а́ккулъ m (ákkul) in 1788, акулъ m (akul) in 1755. Likely inherited from Middle Russian (or possibly a back-formation), attested only as a derivative акулий (akulij) used to describe liver oil of a Greenland shark in a source going back to late
Borrowed from a Sami language; compare Skolt Sami juõigg and Northern Sami juoigat.
Borrowed from a Sami language (compare Northern Sami guvžá and Kildin Sami куввч (kuvvč)), likely via Northern Finnish dialects (kumsi) or Karelian kumša.
A Sami borrowing, ultimately from Proto-Samic *moršë. Compare Finnish mursu, Skolt Sami moršša, English morse, and possibly the second element of translingual Rosmarus.
Borrowed from a Sami language, ultimately from Proto-Samic *pāltēs.

parole.significato: a Sami (member of an indigenous Finno-Ugric people of Lapland)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Sami language; compare Kildin Sami са̄ммь (sāmm’) and Northern Sami sámi. Possibly related to Russian самое́д (samojéd).

parole.significato: a Samoyed (a person belonging to a Samoyedic ethnic group)
parole.testo: From самодин (samodin, used as an autonym by some Nganasan people when speaking Russian), a dialectal variant of самое́д (samojéd, “Samoyed”), ultimately probably from Sami *saam-edne (“land of the people”).

Probably from Sami *saam-edne (“land of the people”); compare to Finnish Suomi (“Finn”). Russian folk etymology derives the term from само- (samo-, “self”) + есть (jestʹ, “to eat”), literally “self-eater”.
From a Sami language. Compare Northern Sami dealljá.
